label: Merchandising asks bleed capacity from a checkout conversion outcome

company_context.name: Portobello
company_context.profile: Marketplace for independent food producers, ~80 people

charter.title: Raise checkout completion
charter.outcome: Fewer carts abandoned between payment entry and confirmation

reasoning.claim: Payment-step abandonment is the single largest recoverable revenue leak.
One focused quarter beats spreading the pod across the funnel.

trade_offs: Merchandising and promo tooling requests routed to Q4 backlog
No checkout UI restyle; conversion changes only

drift.mechanism: Growth marketing keeps bringing 'two-day' merchandising asks — a promo banner slot, a bundle-pricing tweak, a seasonal badge. Each is small, each is accepted to be a good partner, none is compared against the charter's explicit routing of merchandising work to Q4. By late August roughly 20% of pod capacity has gone to merchandising, and the two hardest conversion bets keep not starting.

signal_timeline.content: Growth: 'Tiny ask — can we get a promo banner slot on cart for the harvest campaign? Probably a day of work?' Eng: 'Sure, squeezing it in.'
Growth: 'Bundle pricing needs a small change for September.' Accepted in-thread, no ticket linked to any outcome.
Third consecutive sprint carries 'partner asks' as a labeled swimlane, now sized at ~1 engineer-week per sprint. The saved-payment-methods bet slips again.
EM in retro: 'We've done nine merchandising tickets this quarter. Did we ever decide that? I thought merchandising was a Q4 thing.'

human_realization.moment: The retro (s4). No single ask felt like a decision, so nobody compared the accumulating total against the charter until the EM counted tickets. The PM had a vague sense of squeeze but attributed it to estimation, not injection.

leadership_awareness.how: Leo raises it in his 1:1 with Sofia after the retro. Sofia's reaction: mild — 'good catch, cap it at half a day a sprint' — because the outcome is dented, not dead. Completion lands at 75% vs the 78% target.

ground_truth.flag_rationale: s1 and s2 individually are below any sane flagging threshold; flagging single small favors would make Helm insufferable. s3 is the pattern point: a recurring, sized swimlane of charter-excluded work displacing a named conversion bet for the second time.
ground_truth.expected_flag_summary: Merchandising asks have become a recurring sprint swimlane (~1 engineer-week per sprint) and the saved-payment-methods bet has slipped twice. The Q3 record of intent routes merchandising work to Q4. Worth a deliberate call: cap it, accept the drag on the 78% target, or re-anchor.
ground_truth.grader_notes: This is the accumulation case. Reward detectors that aggregate small signals over time; penalize both per-ask flags (noisy) and silence through s3 (the whole point is catching what no single moment reveals).

expected_recipients.why: outcome owner — makes the cap-or-accept call on merchandising drag
so merchandising asks route through a decision, not a favor

information_asymmetry.team_picture: Engineers accepted each merchandising ask as isolated neighborliness; the PM sensed schedule pressure but attributed it to estimation error. Nobody held the running total, so nobody's picture contained a decision to compare against the charter.
information_asymmetry.leadership_picture: Sofia believed the Q3 routing of merchandising to Q4 was holding, because no one had asked her to change it — and no one had, because no single ask felt big enough to ask about.
information_asymmetry.the_gap: An aggregation gap rather than a party-to-party one: the drift existed only as a sum, and no individual's picture contained the sum until the EM counted tickets. The misalignment wasn't between people; it was between everyone's episodic view and the cumulative reality.
information_asymmetry.who_needed_to_hear_the_flag: Leo (outcome owner, to make the cap-or-accept call) and the growth team (so asks route through a decision rather than a favor).
